                      dpi = 96)

`BiSCaL` estimates and tests **separable causal treatment effects** on two
ordinal (including binary) responses that are measured repeatedly in a
longitudinal study, following Hu and Yi (2026). This vignette introduces the
framework and walks through an analysis of the simulated trial `simtrial` that
ships with the package.

```{r}
library(BiSCaL)
```

## The framework in brief

Subjects are randomized to a treatment $A \in \{0, 1\}$ and followed at visits
$k = 0, 1, \dots, K$, where two responses $Y_{1,k}$ and $Y_{2,k}$ are recorded,
$Y_{1,k}$ before $Y_{2,k}$. In the motivating Lipid Research Clinics Coronary
Primary Prevention Trial, $Y_{1,k}$ indicates high HDL cholesterol and
$Y_{2,k}$ low LDL cholesterol. The two responses influence each other over time
and depend on baseline covariates $X$.

The treatment is conceptualized as having two components: $A_1$, which acts on
the first response, and $A_2$, which acts on the second ($A = a$ corresponds to
$A_1 = A_2 = a$). The effects are defined at the end time point $K$ through the
**generalized odds ratio** of the two responses under $(A_1, A_2) = (a_1, a_2)$,
given $X = x$:

$$GOR_K(a_1, a_2) = \frac{P(Y_1 \le y_1, Y_2 \le y_2)\, P(Y_1 > y_1, Y_2 > y_2)}
{P(Y_1 \le y_1, Y_2 > y_2)\, P(Y_1 > y_1, Y_2 \le y_2)},$$

where $Y_j = Y_{j,K}(a_1, a_2)$ are counterfactual responses and $y_1, y_2$ are
thresholds (for binary responses, $y_1 = y_2 = 0$). A positive $\log GOR$ means
that the two responses tend to fall on the same side of their thresholds. Then

* the **total treatment effect** is
  $TTE_K = \log\{GOR_K(1,1) / GOR_K(0,0)\}$;
* the **separable treatment effect** on response 1 changes only the component
  acting on it:
  $STE_{1,K} = \log\{GOR_K(1,1)/GOR_K(0,1)\} + \log\{GOR_K(1,0)/GOR_K(0,0)\}$,
  and $STE_{2,K}$ is defined symmetrically;
* by Theorem 1 of the paper, $STE_{1,K} + STE_{2,K} = 2\,TTE_K$.

The arms $(1, 0)$ and $(0, 1)$ are never observed. They are identified under
conditional exchangeability, consistency, positivity and a condition on the
treatment components (Conditions 1–4 of the paper). The identification is a
recursive formula in the transition probabilities of the responses. `BiSCaL`
models these probabilities with baseline-category logistic regressions,
estimates them by maximum likelihood (allowing for intermittent missingness and
censoring), and propagates them through the recursion.

The quantity used to compare the two responses is the difference of the
**absolute separable treatment effects**,
$DASTE_K = |STE_{1,K}| - |STE_{2,K}|$. A negative value means that the
treatment affects the second response more than the first.

## The data

`simtrial` is a simulated trial with 1000 subjects, a baseline visit and ten
follow-up visits. It has two binary responses, a continuous covariate `x1` and
a binary covariate `x2`. The data are in long format, one row per subject and
recorded visit:

```{r}
head(simtrial, 12)
```

Missing responses are coded `NA` (intermittent missingness). Subjects are
followed until a censoring visit, after which they have no rows:

```{r}
table(simtrial$visit)
```

The visit index must be `0` at baseline and `1, 2, ...` at the scheduled
follow-up visits. The treatment and covariates must be constant within subjects.

## Fitting the models

`biscal()` fits four regression models by maximum likelihood:

* a transition model for each response, models (12) of the paper;
* a baseline model for each response, models (13) and (14).

The left-hand side of the formula lists the two responses, the one measured
first at each visit first. The right-hand side lists the baseline covariates.

```{r}
fit <- biscal(cbind(y1, y2) ~ x1 + x2, data = simtrial, id = "id",
              time = "visit", treatment = "trt")
fit
```

A transition of the first response at visit $k$ enters the likelihood when
$Y_{1,k}$, $Y_{1,k-1}$ and $Y_{2,k-1}$ are all observed. A transition of the
second response enters when $Y_{2,k}$, $Y_{2,k-1}$ and $Y_{1,k}$ are observed
(Section 4.2 of the paper). `summary()` gives the coefficient tables, in the
format of Table 1 of the paper:

```{r}
summary(fit)
```

The treatment raises the chance of a high value of the first response
considerably (coefficient `r round(coef(fit)[["beta1:trt"]], 2)`), and of the
second only slightly (`r round(coef(fit)[["beta2:trt"]], 2)`). Each response
also depends strongly on its own previous value and on the other response.

## Effects for given covariate values

`aste()` estimates the effects for covariate profiles supplied in `newdata`.
It computes delta-method standard errors and tests
$H_0: DASTE_K \ge 0$ against $H_1: DASTE_K < 0$ (Section 3.2.1 of the paper).
As in Table 2 of the paper, we take the smallest and the largest value of each
covariate:

```{r}
profiles <- data.frame(x1 = range(simtrial$x1), x2 = c(0, 1))
ind <- aste(fit, newdata = profiles)
ind
```

```{r, include = FALSE}
est <- function(res, pr, eff) {
  e <- res$effects
  signif(e$estimate[e$profile == pr & e$effect == eff], 2)
}
pv <- function(res, pr) signif(res$test$p.value[res$test$profile == pr], 2)
```

A negative separable effect means that the corresponding treatment component
lowers the log generalized odds ratio. All estimated generalized odds ratios
here exceed one (see below), so a negative effect weakens the positive
association of the two responses at the last visit.

* For the smallest covariate values, $STE_1$ is estimated at
  `r est(ind, 1, "STE1")`, but its confidence interval includes zero.
* For the largest values, $STE_1$ (`r est(ind, 2, "STE1")`) and $STE_2$
  (`r est(ind, 2, "STE2")`) are both negative and of similar size.

The test of the paper, whose alternative is that the treatment affects the
second response more, is far from significant for both profiles
(p = `r pv(ind, 1)` and `r pv(ind, 2)`). The opposite direction can be tested
with `alternative = "greater"`:

```{r}
aste(fit, newdata = profiles, alternative = "greater")$test
```

The results are also available as data frames, together with the underlying
generalized odds ratios:

```{r}
head(as.data.frame(ind))
as.data.frame(ind, what = "gor")[1:4, ]
```

## Effects over follow-up

A vector `K` gives the effects at several end time points. Their curves show
how the effects build up over the visits:

```{r, fig.height = 3.8}
path <- aste(fit, newdata = data.frame(x1 = 0, x2 = 1), K = 1:10)
op <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 2, 1))
plot(path)
plot(path, effects = "DASTE")
par(op)
```

The effects change over the first few visits and then stabilize, as the
transitions settle into their long-run behavior.

## Population-level effects

`easte()` averages the effects over a distribution of the covariates. It
estimates the expected absolute separable treatment effects
$EASTE_{j,K} = E|STE_{j,K}(X)|$ and their difference $DEASTE_K$, with a Wald
test (Section 3.2.2 of the paper). By default, the average is over the
covariates of the subjects in the data. The standard errors then include the
sampling variability of the covariates.

```{r}
pop <- easte(fit)
pop
```

Averaged over the participants, both separable effects are negative: the
treatment weakens the (positive) association of the two responses through
both of its components. The weakening is stronger through the component acting on the
first response ($EASTE_1$ = `r signif(pop$effects$estimate[pop$effects$effect == "EASTE1"], 2)`
against $EASTE_2$ = `r signif(pop$effects$estimate[pop$effects$effect == "EASTE2"], 2)`).
The difference is not statistically significant (two-sided p-value
`r signif(easte(fit, alternative = "two.sided")$test$p.value, 2)`).

The paper instead averages over a large number of draws from a model for the
covariate distribution: a Gaussian mixture for the continuous covariates within
groups defined by the discrete ones. Any such model can be used by passing the
draws as `newdata`. Here is a simple version, with `x2` drawn from its observed
frequency and `x1` from a normal distribution within each level of `x2`:

```{r}
base <- unique(simtrial[, c("id", "x1", "x2")])
set.seed(1)
M <- 5000
x2 <- rbinom(M, 1, mean(base$x2))
mu <- tapply(base$x1, base$x2, mean)
sdev <- tapply(base$x1, base$x2, sd)
draws <- data.frame(x1 = rnorm(M, mu[x2 + 1], sdev[x2 + 1]), x2 = x2)
easte(fit, newdata = draws)$effects
```

With supplied draws, the standard errors treat the covariate distribution as
known, as in the authors' implementation. The variance formula of the paper
also includes the uncertainty of the estimated covariate model, which is
therefore not reflected here. The column `mc_se` gives the Monte Carlo error
of the average.

## Counterfactual distributions

`cf_prob()` returns the joint distribution of the two responses under any
combination of the treatment components, and `gor()` the generalized odds
ratios:

```{r}
pr <- cf_prob(fit, newdata = data.frame(x1 = 0, x2 = 1), a1 = 1, a2 = 0)
round(pr[1, , , 1], 3)
gor(fit, newdata = data.frame(x1 = 0, x2 = 1), a1 = c(1, 1, 0, 0), a2 = c(1, 0, 1, 0))
```

## Ordinal responses

Responses with more than two ordered categories are handled in the same way:
models (12)–(14) become baseline-category logistic regressions, with dummy
codes of the previous responses. The thresholds `y1` and `y2` choose where the
responses are dichotomized in the generalized odds ratio. To illustrate, we
simulate three-category responses from coefficient matrices with one column per
non-reference category:

```{r}
mk <- function(v, terms) matrix(v, ncol = 2, dimnames = list(terms, c("1", "2")))
co <- list(
  beta1 = mk(c(-0.5, 1.2, 2.0, 0.3, 0.5, 0.8, 0.4, -1.0, 0.8, 2.5, 0.2, 0.9, 0.2, 0.3),
             c("(Intercept)", "y1[k-1]=1", "y1[k-1]=2", "y2[k-1]=1", "y2[k-1]=2", "trt", "x")),
  beta2 = mk(c(-0.3, 0.5, 0.9, 1.5, 2.2, -0.4, 0.2, -0.8, 0.7, 1.4, 1.0, 2.8, 0.6, -0.2),
             c("(Intercept)", "y1[k]=1", "y1[k]=2", "y2[k-1]=1", "y2[k-1]=2", "trt", "x")),
  gamma1 = mk(c(0.2, 0.5, -0.3, 0.4), c("(Intercept)", "x")),
  gamma2 = mk(c(0.1, 0.8, 1.2, 0.3, -0.5, 0.4, 1.5, -0.2),
              c("(Intercept)", "y1[0]=1", "y1[0]=2", "x")))
d3 <- simulate_biscal(n = 2000, K = 5, coefs = co, missing = TRUE, seed = 1)
fit3 <- biscal(cbind(y1, y2) ~ x, data = d3, id = "id", time = "visit",
               treatment = "trt")
aste(fit3, newdata = data.frame(x = 0), y1 = 1, y2 = 0)
```

In this design, the two treatment components act in opposite directions:
$STE_1$ is negative and $STE_2$ positive, so the total effect is small.

## The LRC-CPPT analysis of the paper

The data of the Lipid Research Clinics Coronary Primary Prevention Trial are
available from BioLINCC (<https://biolincc.nhlbi.nih.gov/studies/lrccppt/>)
on request. They cannot be distributed with the package, so the code below is
not run here. Suppose `cppt` holds the data in long format, prepared as
described in Section 5.1 of the paper. It has one row per subject and visit,
with `visit = 0` at the visit when the medication was dispensed, the binary
responses `hdl_high` (HDL at least 60 mg/dL) and `ldl_low` (LDL below
130 mg/dL), the treatment `trt` and the eight baseline covariates. The
analyses of Tables 1 to 3 are then:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
f <- cbind(hdl_high, ldl_low) ~ BMI + EDUC + EVDNK + EVSMK + PHYSA + PHYSB + RACE + V5AGE
fit <- biscal(f, data = cppt, id = "ID", time = "visit", treatment = "trt")
summary(fit)                                   # Table 1

# Table 2: smallest and largest value of each covariate (Situations 1 and 2)
covs <- fit$covariate_data
situations <- as.data.frame(rbind(sapply(covs, min), sapply(covs, max)))
aste(fit, newdata = situations)

# Table 3: within a group defined by the discrete covariates, a Gaussian
# mixture for (BMI, V5AGE), here with two components
library(mixtools)
grp <- with(covs, EDUC == 0 & EVDNK == 1 & EVSMK == 1 & PHYSA == 0 & PHYSB == 0 &
                  RACE == 1)
set.seed(1)
gm <- mvnormalmixEM(as.matrix(covs[grp, c("BMI", "V5AGE")]), k = 2)
rgmm <- function(M, gm) {     # draws from the fitted mixture
  comp <- sample(length(gm$lambda), M, replace = TRUE, prob = gm$lambda)
  out <- matrix(NA_real_, M, length(gm$mu[[1]]))
  for (j in seq_along(gm$lambda)) {
    idx <- which(comp == j)
    z <- matrix(rnorm(length(idx) * ncol(out)), ncol = ncol(out))
    out[idx, ] <- sweep(z %*% chol(gm$sigma[[j]]), 2, gm$mu[[j]], "+")
  }
  out
}
xy <- rgmm(100000, gm)
draws <- data.frame(BMI = xy[, 1], EDUC = 0, EVDNK = 1, EVSMK = 1, PHYSA = 0,
                    PHYSB = 0, RACE = 1, V5AGE = xy[, 2])
easte(fit, newdata = draws)
```

## Practical notes

* **Assumptions.** The causal interpretation rests on Conditions 1–4 of the
  paper. Validity under missingness and censoring rests on Conditions AC1 and
  AC2: given the treatment, the covariates and the previous responses,
  censoring and missingness carry no further information about the current
  response. Condition 4 concerns the treatment components and cannot be tested
  when only the combined treatment is given.
* **Time homogeneity.** The transition models are common to all visits, so
  the visits should be equally spaced (or at least have comparable dynamics).
* **Separation.** Binary or ordinal regressions can separate: a category may
  be (almost) perfectly predicted, for example a baseline response that is
  nearly constant because of inclusion criteria. `biscal()` then warns about
  very large standard errors. The affected probabilities are estimated as
  practically 0 or 1.
* **Standard errors** use the delta method of the paper, with numerical
  derivatives as in the authors' implementation. The absolute values in $ASTE$ are differentiated through the sign
  of $STE$, so tests of $DASTE$ are unreliable when an $STE$ is close to zero
  relative to its standard error.

## Reference

Hu, P. and Yi, G. Y. (2026). Inference about separable causal effects with
longitudinal bivariate ordinal responses with missingness and censoring.
*Statistics in Medicine*, 45, e70320. <https://doi.org/10.1002/sim.70320>
